claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy-alloy microstructure consists of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The initial lamellar microstructure contains numerous internal boundaries.
A hierarchical microstructure with optimized colony size and boundary density can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Hierarchical microstructure design can produce optimized colony size and boundary density.
Optimizing colony size and boundary density reduces microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Optimizing colony size and boundary density improves strain hardening.
Reduced microcracking increases room-temperature tensile ductility relative to an unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
Improved strain hardening increases strength relative to an unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The intervention is limited by the ability of processing techniques to control and optimize colony size and boundary density.
The relationship among colony size, boundary density, and mechanical properties is not well understood.
Room-temperature tensile tests across varying colony sizes and boundary densities can evaluate the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a significant improvement in both strength and ductility would falsify the hypothesis.
